extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers, faculty, postdocs and graduate students interested in mentoring, coaching, and grant-writing support
extracted.subtask_description: Discussion of using professional or informal coaching/mentoring to improve researchers' skills (manuscript and grant review/writing, advising, collaboration, leadership). Focus is on whether coaching models from other fields could be applied in academia and practical ways to implement them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Career-long professional coaching model
rubrics_metrics.description: “The coaching model [is] what you think of with athletes and singers, who have someone who coaches them all the way through their career, even if they’re one of the best in the world... In his case, his wife … He said he had a coach his entire career.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: high-performing professionals benefit from continuous coaching; implication for academia is that violinists/surgeons (and by extension researchers) might also benefit from career-long coaching rather than the assumption that graduation + practice will suffice. Use examples from other fields to justify adopting long-term coaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent, candid critique as core coaching function
rubrics_metrics.description: Coaching provides someone who can consistently critique you even though you think you are on top of your game can really improve matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coaching should include regular, honest critique of work (manuscripts, grants). A coach's persistent critical perspective is valuable even for experienced researchers and can reveal blind spots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mentors/senior faculty as de facto coaches for juniors
rubrics_metrics.description: “Aren’t ‘mentors’, i.e. senior faculty supposed to fill that role, at least for the newbies?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize existing mentoring structures: senior colleagues often provide manuscript and grant critique. Evaluate whether formal coaching adds value beyond traditional mentoring, and design coaching to complement rather than replace mentorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty brown-bag / informal study-section as practical coaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Faculty brownbag lunch series where all faculty give research presentations serves as an informal study section/review panel and has proved extremely valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended implementation: create regular internal forums (brown-bag talks) where colleagues present manuscripts or grant ideas for group critique. Benefits include peer review practice, creation of an intellectual environment, and material to document NIH 'Environment – Contribution to Success' or 'Facilities and Other Resources – Other' sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coaching targeted to grant-writing specifics (R01s are different)
rubrics_metrics.description: “R01s are a different beast….there is time to critique someone else’s proposal while you are putting together yours for the same deadline.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant coaching should account for grant-specific constraints (deadlines, review conventions). Peer review timings and grant-specific expertise matter; set up review cycles and mock study-sections calibrated to funding program expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coaching located outside hierarchical relationships reduces barriers
rubrics_metrics.description: “I would guess that some of the success of coaching comes from its positioning outside the ranks of boss and trainee. Neither a job nor one’s hold on power is threatened by outside coaching.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design coaching to be independent of formal supervisory lines so participants feel safe admitting weaknesses. External or neutral coaches can provide frank feedback without threatening career relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coaching for non-research leadership and professional skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Many faculty are hired for their success in research, and promptly made managers. Does the title of Professor somehow automatically make you a good communicator, a good organizer, a good team leader? I would guess that many labs would run a lot better with some coaching in these areas, in which we receive so little training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include training/coaching modules on communication, lab organization, team leadership, and management — skills often not covered in traditional academic training but important for running labs and collaborative projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coaching as ad hoc or short-term targeted intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: “I come and go, like the guy you take a lesson from to improve one aspect of your swing.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coaching can be episodic: offer short-term, focused coaching engagements (e.g., one-off sessions to improve a specific grant section or writing problem) as an alternative to ongoing coaching relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coaches as confidential safe spaces for issues trainees can't raise with chairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Coaches can field questions they feel they can’t discuss with their chairs or anyone in their tenure line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coaching services should offer confidentiality so trainees and junior faculty can seek candid advice on sensitive topics (career concerns, conflicts, tenure-related questions) that they might not raise with supervisors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh potential downsides of coaching
rubrics_metrics.description: A counterpoint: what, if any, down-sides are there to coaching?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When implementing coaching, evaluate possible negatives (cost, dependency, coaching quality, conflicts with mentorship, confidentiality breaches). Build safeguards: vet coaches, set scopes, preserve mentorship responsibilities, and ensure coaching supplements rather than supplants institutional support.
